doc.title: Jack Sheldon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Lessons with Uan Rasey
summary: Studying trumpet and singing recently to hit notes on the pitch.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Wow. Have you ever had over the years, had to change your physical approach to trumpet playing?

Well I started taking lessons about ten years ago I guess, something like that, with Uan Rasey. And he’s helped me. I’m still playing about the same way that I always did, but he’s helped me a lot with my range and everything. I’m still taking from him. I’ll take for the rest of my life now. I studied singing with his daughter, who works with the L.A. Opera, Luanna. So yeah, he’s changed me. He’d like to change me more and get me to hit the note right on the head instead of coming up to it, I do that a lot, I have to watch that.
Do you know you’re doing it?

No. I mean and then he’ll stop me and say, “No, hit it right on the head.” I have a tendency, I guess it’s jazz or just a habit of — getting up to the pitch. And he stops me and he wants it right on the pitch, which is much more difficult for me.
Yeah. It’s almost like an ear thing too, isn’t it?
Yeah. And so you hear it first, and I don’t know where it got in that habit.
